definition: A walk in which no edge is used more than once, although vertices may be repeated.
A walk in which no vertex is visited more than once, so no edge is repeated either.
A trail that starts and finishes at the same vertex, so it is closed and repeats no edge.
A circuit that repeats no vertex, except that the start vertex is also the end vertex.
A vertex whose degree is odd; every graph has an even number of odd vertices.
A trail that uses every edge of a graph exactly once; a connected graph has one exactly when it has 0 or 2 odd vertices, and with 2 odd vertices the trail starts at one and finishes at the other.
A circuit that uses every edge of a graph exactly once; a connected graph has one exactly when every vertex has even degree.
A path that visits every vertex of a graph exactly once; there is no simple test for whether one exists.
A cycle that visits every vertex of a graph exactly once and returns to its start vertex.
A subgraph of a connected graph that is a tree and includes every vertex of the graph.
A spanning tree of a connected weighted graph with the least possible total weight; there may be more than one, all with the same weight.
A way to find a minimum spanning tree: take the edges in increasing order of weight, add each one unless it makes a cycle, and stop at $n - 1$ edges for $n$ vertices.

A way to find a minimum spanning tree: from a start vertex, keep adding the least-weight edge from a vertex in the tree to a vertex not yet in it; it can be run directly on a table (the matrix method).
Finding the least-weight closed route along every edge of a connected weighted graph at least once, by repeating the shortest routes for the least-weight pairing of the odd vertices.
Finding the Hamiltonian cycle of least total weight in a weighted complete graph; a practical problem is first turned into one with a table of least distances.
A table giving the weight of the shortest route, direct or not, between every pair of vertices; it turns a practical travelling salesman problem into the classical one on a complete graph.
Building a tour by going from the start to the nearest unvisited vertex each time, then back to the start; its weight is an upper bound for the travelling salesman problem, not always the best tour.

Deleting one vertex, finding a minimum spanning tree of the rest and adding the two least-weight edges from the deleted vertex; the total is a lower bound for the travelling salesman problem, and the largest such bound is the best.
